scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

Let me break down the situation step by step. First, the person is engaged and planning a small, semi-formal beach wedding. Their mother wants to go wedding dress shopping together and has booked an appointment at a fancy bridal shop that only does white dresses. The person doesn't want a white dress and has already looked up the shop, knowing it's only white. They think the whole white wedding dress thing is stupid, starting with Queen Victoria, and that the symbolism of white as pure or innocent is outdated. The main reason they don't want a white dress is that their mother wore white and got divorced. They mention that every other woman in the family wore colored dresses and had long, mostly happy marriages. When the mother asks why they don't want white, the person first gives the Queen Victoria line, which the mother dismisses. Then they mention not being innocent, which leads to an awkward conversation. The mother presses further, and the person finally says it's because the mother was the only one to break the tradition and got divorced, which makes them not confident in white dresses. The mother gets really quiet, starts crying, and says she tried her best, feeling that the person spoke to her cruelly, especially since the divorce was upsetting. The person hasn't apologized yet and feels the mother backed them into a corner, making them justify their choice when it's their wedding and their choice. So, is the person AITA? Let's consider both sides. On one hand, the person is planning their own wedding and should have the right to choose their dress. They have valid reasons, both personal and symbolic, for not wanting white. They tried to give other reasons first, but the mother kept pressing for the real reason, leading to the emotional conversation. On the other hand, the person's choice of words and the way they handled the situation might have been hurtful. The mother is likely sensitive about the divorce, and bringing it up in this context could have been insensitive, especially in front of others or in a way that made the mother feel attacked. The person feels that they shouldn't have had to justify their choice, but the mother, as a parent, might feel entitled to understand such a significant decision. However, the way the person handled the conversation, especially the part about not being innocent and the divorce, could have been handled more gently. In conclusion, while the person has the right to choose their wedding dress, the way they communicated their reasons, especially the personal and emotional ones, might have been unnecessarily hurtful. They could have approached the conversation with more empathy and understanding, considering the mother's feelings about the divorce. Therefore, the person might be AITA because their approach, though justified, could have been handled more sensitively.
